Detects PostgreSQL query performance regressions and pinpoints which Kubernetes deployment caused them.

Try it in your browser Install How it works

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Teams running Postgres on Kubernetes (CloudNativePG, Zalando, Crunchy, Percona...) deploy applications many times a day via GitOps (ArgoCD, Flux, Argo Rollouts). When query latency spikes, the first question in every post-mortem is:

Which deploy caused this?

Answered by hand, today

  • Open Grafana
  • Look at pg_stat_statements
  • Try to recall when the last deploy happened
  • Cross-reference timestamps by eye

Few tools connect those dots for you.

pg-regression-radar does.

docs.title: Our math
docs.text:
Abstract

A PerformanceRegression is a verdict reached in seven steps from two cumulative counters. This note derives each step, states the assumptions it needs and measures where they fail. The figures run the engine's own arithmetic, in your browser.

f≥1+θ |τˆ−td|≤τ p≤α

docs.title: DerivationFrom counters to samplesThe number PostgreSQL shows is not the number we analyse.
docs.text: interval mean xtcumulative mean T/C Step Step lands at Counter reset

docs.title: §1Interval means
docs.text:
pg_stat_statements exposes two monotone counters per query: the calls C and the total execution time T in milliseconds, both accumulated since the last reset. Its mean_exec_time is their ratio, which is a mean over the whole history. We scrape both counters and analyse the mean of the calls made since the previous scrape:

xt=Tt−Tt−1Ct−Ct−1=ΔTtΔCt

The cumulative mean is slow for a precise reason. If a query ran npre calls at mean μ and then npost calls at μ+δ, the counter reports

TC=μ+δ·npostnpre+npost

so after a deploy it moves only by the share of calls made since. A step of +100% needs as many calls after the deploy as before it just to read +50%. The interval mean reads the step at the next scrape.

Resets

A counter that goes down (a restart, pg_stat_statements_reset(), a change in stats_since) makes ΔC negative. That interval is discarded, not clamped, because its calls belong to no window. The cumulative mean jumps at a reset; the interval means do not.

docs.title: DerivationGates before statisticsFloors decide when we are allowed to answer, not how often the answer is wrong.
docs.text: Per-call CV Calls in the window Scrapes in the window

docs.title: §2Floors and the pre-filter
docs.text:
Both windows (before and after the deploy) must clear two floors. Samples protect the machinery: the t-test and the energy statistic estimate a spread from the data, so they need points, n≥nmin=10. Executions bound the precision of the window's mean: the standard error of a mean of N calls with per-call coefficient of variation CV is

SE(x¯)/μ=CVN

With N=100 and CV=1, a window mean is good to about ±10% at one standard error. Windows with fewer calls return InsufficientData, which is different from NoRegression: the first says "we could not tell".

The pre-filter compares the call-weighted window means, x¯=∑ΔT∑ΔC, and stops when

f−1<θ=0.20⟹NoRegression

It is an optimisation and a guard: the expensive stages run only on shifts big enough to matter.

docs.title: Stage 1Finding the change with energyE-divisive means asks whether two stretches of the series come from the same distribution, not only whether their means differ.
docs.text: left of the splitright of the splitargmax Q Shift in the middle Noise

docs.title: §3The energy statistic
docs.text:
For two samples A=a1…ana and B=b1…bnb let D(A,B) be the mean absolute distance across them. The energy distance of Székely and Rizzo [1] compares the cross distance with the distances inside each sample:

ℰ=2Dab−Daa−DbbDab=1nanb∑i,j|ai−bj|

It is zero exactly when the two samples have the same distribution (in the limit) and grows with any difference: location, spread or shape. Scaled by the sample sizes it becomes the statistic the engine evaluates at every admissible split k of the series, with within-sample distances averaged over unordered pairs [2]:

Q(k)=2nanbna+nb(Dab−Daa2−Dbb2)τˆ=argmaxm≤k≤n−mQ(k)

Here na=k, nb=n−k, and m=max(3,⌊n/10⌋) keeps a change from being "found" in the first or last few points. A split is kept only if Q>0. Evaluating all splits costs O(n2) because moving the split one step changes each sum by one row and one column.

Why not just split at the deploy?

Rolling deploys and connection draining spread the shift over minutes, and the collector adds scrape granularity. Letting the data place the split gives the shift's real start, and the next stage asks whether that start is close enough to the deploy to blame it.

docs.title: Stage 1bWas it this deploy?A change point is only evidence about a deploy if it is close to it.
docs.text: Window W Located change τˆ

docs.title: §4The tolerance window
docs.text:
Let td be the deploy time and τˆ the located change. The change is attributed to the deploy only if

|τˆ−td|≤τ=max(2 min,0.2W)

where W is the analysis window. Making the allowance a fraction of the window keeps the same relative slack for a tight 10-minute window and a loose 60-minute one; the floor keeps short windows from shrinking it to nothing.

The order matters. The engine checks the tolerance before the significance test, so a shift that is very significant but starts twenty minutes before the deploy is reported as unrelated background change, never as a regression of this deploy. This is the step that turns a change detector into an attribution tool.

A trade-off, not a free parameter

A wide tolerance catches slow rollouts and attributes more unrelated shifts to the deploy. A narrow one does the opposite. Under a Poisson process of unrelated shifts the expected number of coincidences grows linearly in τ.

docs.title: Stage 2Is it more than noise?Welch's t-test on the two segments the data itself found.
docs.text: Change in the mean Interval-mean CV Points before Points after

docs.title: §5Welch's t-test
docs.text:
The two segments on either side of τˆ are compared without assuming equal variances. A latency regression often changes the spread as well as the mean, so the pooled-variance Student test would be the wrong tool [3]:

t=x¯b−x¯asa2na+sb2nb

The reference distribution is Student's t with the Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom,

ν=(sa2na+sb2nb)2(sa2/na)2na−1+(sb2/nb)2nb−1

and the two-sided p-value has a closed form through the regularised incomplete beta function, which is what the engine computes with a continued fraction [4]:

p=P(|Tν|≥|t|)=Iν/(ν+t2)(ν2,12)

The test is applied to the per-interval means xt, not to individual calls. By the central limit theorem those are much closer to normal than the heavy-tailed per-call latencies, which is why a test that assumes normality is defensible here at all.

docs.title: InterpretationWhat the score meansconfidenceScore is 1 − p. It ranks detections. It is not the probability that the regression is real.
docs.text: p-value

docs.title: §6A p-value is not a posterior
docs.text:
The p-value answers "if nothing changed, how often would noise alone look at least this extreme?". Reading 1−p as "the chance the change is real" inverts the conditional. How far apart the two can be is bounded, without any assumption about the prior, by the calibration of Sellke, Bayarri and Berger [5]. For p<1/e the Bayes factor in favour of "no change" is at least B(p)=−eplnp, so with even prior odds

P(H0∣data)≥(1+1−eplnp)−1 p score 1 − p P(no change) ≥ 0.05 0.95 0.29 0.01 0.99 0.11 0.001 0.999 0.018 0.0001 0.9999 0.0025

A score of 0.95 can leave a 29% chance that nothing changed. That is why the score is documented as a ranking and a threshold input, and why it should not be quoted as a probability.

docs.title: CaveatThe search inflates significanceChoosing the split from the data, then testing it as if it had been chosen in advance, is optimistic.
docs.text:
Points per series Autocorrelation φ

Dashed line: what a correctly calibrated test would give.

docs.title: §7Maximally selected statistics
docs.text:
Stage 1 picks the split with the largest Q. Stage 2 then tests that split with a t-test whose reference distribution assumes the split was fixed beforehand. Under "no change" a t-statistic at a fixed split has p∼Uniform(0,1), but the split k∗ that maximises a separation statistic is by construction the one where the two sides look most different, so the p-value pk∗ at that split is too small:

P(pk∗≤α∣H0)>α

The statistical literature calls this the problem of maximally selected statistics and corrects for it with a p-value that accounts for the search [6]. E-divisive means itself does so with a permutation test over the whole search [1].

The figure draws series with no change at all, applies stages 1 and 2 exactly as the engine does, and histograms the p-values. A correct test would be flat. With independent noise the lab typically puts 35–39% of them below 0.05; with autocorrelated noise, far more.

What protects production

Three other gates sit around this one: the pre-filter (a real +20% is required), the tolerance (the located change must sit near the deploy) and the floors. Through the whole pipeline the measured share of no-change analyses reported as Detected is much lower than the raw p-value rate; the roadmap tracks the calibration work.

docs.title: DesignHow many calls you needSensitivity is bought with executions. This is the price list.
docs.text: Per-call CV Smallest change δ

docs.title: §8Sample size for a target effect
docs.text:
To detect a relative change δ in the mean at size α=0.05 (two-sided) with power 1−β=0.8, a two-sample comparison needs, per window,

N≈2(zα/2+zβ)2CV2δ2=15.7CV2δ2

using zα/2=1.96 and zβ=0.84. The cost is quadratic in both noise and ambition: halving the smallest change you care about quadruples the calls you need. A query with CV = 1 needs about 390 calls per window to see +20% reliably, and about 1,570 to see +10%.

This is the asymptotic normal approximation for means, and it ignores the search of §7, so it is optimistic for small windows. Treat it as a lower bound when choosing --min-executions and the window length.

docs.title: HonestyWhere the math stopsThe two assumptions that matter most, and what happens when they fail.
docs.text:
Independent intervals

The t-test and the permutation argument assume the interval means are independent. Serially correlated noise (a slow checkpoint, a cache warming) inflates the false-positive rate, as the selection lab shows with φ > 0.

Counters, not calls

The mean of an interval hides its composition: a shift in the mix of parameter values looks the same as a slower plan. That is why a detection carries a plan diff and an externalCauseSuspected flag.

docs.title: ReproducibilityThe page runs the engine's mathNot a re-implementation we hope is close.
docs.text:
Every widget above calls one dependency-free module, docs/assets/math/math-core.js, a line-by-line port of internal/correlation/engine.go: the interval means, the minimum segment length, the incremental energy statistic, the Lanczos log-gamma, the incomplete beta continued fraction and the decision order of evaluateQuery. A Go test (internal/correlation/mathpage_test.go) feeds fixed series, generated by that module, to the real engine and fails if the verdict, the change point, t, ν or p differ, so the page cannot drift from the code without CI noticing. Noise in the lab is a seeded log-normal per call (so the mean of c calls has coefficient of variation CV/c), with optional AR(1) correlation, from a fixed seed so every figure is reproducible.

For the full operational description of each stage, flag and CRD field, see the Detection Algorithm and the Configuration Reference. To run the engine itself on a workload, open the Playground.

docs.title: Playground
docs.text: Run the real detection engine against a real PostgreSQL, entirely in your browser: no Postgres, no Kubernetes, no install.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The playground runs a small SQL workload against PostgreSQL with pg_stat_statements enabled, applies a "deploy" halfway through, and feeds what the collector would have scraped to pg-regression-radar's correlation engine. Pick a scenario, change the traffic or the thresholds, or write your own schema, workload and deploy, and see which queries the engine flags and why.

Nothing is sent to a server. Everything runs in your browser tab.

The playground needs JavaScript and WebAssembly.

docs.title: What you are looking at
docs.text:
The chart shows one query's latency over the 22 simulated minutes. Two lines tell the story that motivated the engine's design:

  • The dashed line is pg_stat_statements.mean_exec_time, the average of every call since the counters were last reset. It moves slowly after a regression, and jumps for no reason after a reset.
  • The solid line is the mean latency of only the calls made since the previous scrape, derived from the cumulative calls and total_exec_time counters. This is what the engine analyses. See Collector Internals and Detection Algorithm.

The table gives the engine's verdict per query. InsufficientData means the query ran too rarely in one of the windows for either answer to be trustworthy; see --min-samples and --min-executions in the Configuration Reference.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
PGlite (PostgreSQL in WebAssembly)        Go engine compiled to WebAssembly
  workload + deploy SQL                     internal/correlation
        |                                          ^
        v                                          |
  pg_stat_statements --snapshot every 30 s--> intervals, change point, t-test
  • PostgreSQL is PGlite running PostgreSQL 18 compiled to WebAssembly, with the real pg_stat_statements extension. It is loaded on first use from the jsDelivr CDN (about 5 MB compressed).
  • The engine is the same internal/correlation package the operator runs, compiled with GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm (about 1 MB compressed) from main. The playground is not tied to a release: it is rebuilt from the main branch on every merge, so it can be a little ahead of the latest release.
  • Time is virtual. The simulation executes the workload as fast as it can and stamps each snapshot as if it were taken every 30 seconds, so a 22-minute scenario takes a few seconds.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Timings are not production timings. A browser tab running PostgreSQL in WebAssembly is far slower than a server and its timings are noisier. The playground shows how the engine reasons about a latency series, not what your database will do.
  • One database, one process. There is no replication, connection pooling, I/O contention or autovacuum behaviour of a real cluster.
  • No plan capture and no alerting. The playground covers detection; plan diffs (--capture-plans), alert delivery and deploy-event sources need a real cluster. See Getting Started.
  • Browser support. A current Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari (16.4 or later).

docs.title: Roadmap items
docs.text:
StatisticsQ1 2027 Welch's t-test ignores how many calls stand behind each observation

Stage 2 weighs a one-call interval like a ten-thousand-call one, while the reported window means are call-weighted.

Read moreShow less

The reported MeanLatencyBefore/MeanLatencyAfter are total time over total calls, but the t-test compares unweighted per-interval means. A ratio-estimator test (mean = total time / total calls, with a cluster-robust variance that treats each scrape interval as a cluster) is consistent with the reported numbers and, in simulation with bursty traffic and log-normal latency, kept the 5% size while raising power for a +30% regression from 41% to 73% at 3 calls per interval. It would also make --min-executions act directly on the precision of the test. Per-call variance from stddev_exec_time is a further input that is not used yet.

ValidationQ4 2026 Neither kind-based e2e workflow has a real GitHub Actions run yet

Both kind-based workflows were validated locally but have never run on a real GitHub Actions runner.

Read moreShow less

.github/workflows/e2e-kind.yml and .github/workflows/e2e-kind-multicluster.yml were both authored, actionlint/YAML-checked, and validated against real clusters in a local sandbox that lacks GitHub Actions' kernel support for kind/Docker-in-Docker (see Multi-Cluster: Operational considerations for the networking workaround that local validation needed) — but neither has actually executed as a real workflow_dispatch/labeled-PR run on an actual GitHub Actions runner. Treat each workflow's first real run as part of reviewing the change that introduces it, not as an already-passing check.

Required checks only have effect once main's ruleset requires each one by name.

Read moreShow less

See Branch Protection — the CI checks in CI/CD only have real effect once main's ruleset actually requires each one by name.

OperationsQ4 2026 GitHub Discussions link

The issue template links to Discussions; whether it is enabled on the repo hasn't been confirmed.

Read moreShow less

.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/config.yml links to the repo's Discussions tab; whether Discussions is actually enabled on the repo hasn't been confirmed.

StatisticsQ1 2027 The Welch's t-test is applied to segments chosen by the same data

The significance test runs on a split the same data picked, so its p-value is optimistic. Calibrate it before reading it as a 5% rate.

Read moreShow less

Stage 1 searches every candidate split for the best E-divisive change point and stage 2 then tests that split as if it had been chosen independently, which makes the p-value optimistic (post-selection inference). The stage 0 pre-filter and the LatencyChangeThreshold mask most of the effect on typical series, but the p-value should not be read as a calibrated 5% false-positive rate: measured with the project's own E-divisive and Welch code on no-change series, 35-39% had p < 0.05 with independent noise and 60-99% with autocorrelated noise, and through the full engine up to 8% of no-change analyses were reported Detected with autocorrelated, heavy-tailed noise. Options, roughly in order of cost: a minimum effect-size floor alongside the p-value; empirical calibration against recorded no-regression series; a permutation test that repeats the full change-point search on each permuted series. Series with autocorrelated noise are the case most worth measuring first.

AttributionQ1 2027 Attribution is by time proximity only, and the proximity check is symmetric

A shift before the deploy can still be blamed on it. Make the window asymmetric, depending on how the event was timestamped.

Read moreShow less

evaluateQuery rejects a change point only when its absolute distance from the deploy exceeds ChangePointTolerance, so a shift that happened before the event can still be attributed to it. That is sometimes right — the ArgoCD and Argo Rollouts parsers stamp DeployEvent.Timestamp with time.Now() when the webhook arrives (typically at sync completion), while the real effect can start when the first replicas roll — and sometimes wrong. Detection Algorithm currently justifies the tolerance only by effects lagging a deploy, which is the opposite case. Planned direction: an asymmetric window whose lead and lag depend on how the event's timestamp was obtained. The OTLP source already lets an operator choose the span's start or end; the webhook sources have no equivalent, so a lightweight first step is to record a timestamp-quality indicator (source-provided vs. receipt time) on the event rather than adding separate started/completed fields to the public DeployEvent type.

AttributionQ1 2027 No way to say "several deploys could explain this."

When several deploys could explain a change, say so with an Ambiguous result instead of presenting one as the cause.

Read moreShow less

Engine.Analyse evaluates one event at a time and every tracked query is a candidate for every event on the same watch — nothing links a queryid to an application, and pg_stat_statements does not record one. Two deploys inside one tolerance window therefore each produce their own regression for the same change point. A first step that needs no new data: when more than one event falls inside the window, mark the result Ambiguous and list the candidate events instead of presenting one as the cause. Further outcomes (Unattributed when no event is close enough, InsufficientEvidence) and candidate ranking by cluster, namespace, and workload can follow once that vocabulary exists.

AttributionQ1 2027 No signal for "everything got slower."

Report how many other queries shifted at the same moment, to tell a deploy-local change from a saturated database.

Read moreShow less

Whether a regression is local to one query or shared by most tracked queries at the same moment is already computable from data the collector holds, and separates "this deploy changed this query" from "the database is saturated". Reporting the fraction of other tracked queries that shifted at the same change point is a cheap first control signal; richer workload context (CPU, connections, lock waits, I/O) is deliberately not planned until there is evidence the cheaper signal is not enough, since requiring it would raise the barrier to adoption.

ValidationQ1 2027 No real ArgoCD or pg_store_plans in the kind + CloudNativePG e2e

The CloudNativePG e2e posts a generic webhook instead of a real ArgoCD one, and runs without pg_store_plans.

Read moreShow less

The kind + CloudNativePG e2e workflow (.github/workflows/e2e-kind.yml) posts a sourceType: generic webhook directly to the DeploySource route rather than standing up ArgoCD's Application controller and Notifications engine (the part that actually emits a real on-sync-succeeded webhook — see Deploy Sources & Webhooks); that's a second, mostly-orthogonal integration surface, a natural follow-up once someone needs to validate ArgoCD's own webhook delivery specifically. Separately, it doesn't run with pg_store_plans on the CloudNativePG instance: that C extension isn't compiled into CloudNativePG's default operand images, and building/maintaining a custom operand image just for this smoke test hasn't been judged worth it yet (narrower than "is pg_store_plans validated against a real server at all" — see Testing for that validation, which runs outside of CloudNativePG specifically).

IntegrationsQ1 2027 PR comments and Grafana annotations

GitHub/GitLab PR comment on detected regression; Grafana annotation.

ValidationQ1 2027 External-user quickstart validation is reproducibly documented but not auto-provable from code alone

Step 7 of the checklist needs a real operator run in an external environment, which code alone can't prove.

Read moreShow less

The execution checklist exists in Quickstart Validation, but completion still depends on a real human/operator run in an external environment.

StatisticsQ2 2027 No multiple-comparison control across queries

Up to 500 queries are tested per pass with no correction. Options: false-discovery-rate control, or ranking by impact.

Read moreShow less

One Analyse or AnalysePeriodic pass can evaluate up to the top 500 queries, each against PValueThreshold, and periodic analysis repeats that on every tick. A false-discovery-rate correction (Benjamini-Hochberg is the obvious first candidate) is one option; ranking and surfacing regressions by their share of total execution time is another that also helps operators triage. Whichever is chosen, the more conservative behaviour should be a separate mode, not a silent change to what PValueThreshold means.

Plan-diffQ2 2027 planner.Diff compares only the root node type, total estimated cost, and snapshot source

The diff only compares the root node, total cost and source. Walking the whole plan tree would explain the “why”.

Read moreShow less

A root that stays an Index Scan while its row estimate moves by four orders of magnitude, or a join order change below an unchanged root, is invisible to it. Walking the whole plan tree — scan types, index names, join methods and order, estimated rows, and sorts — would make the hint far more useful for the "why". Actual rows and buffer counts are only worth adding for sources that record them; EXPLAIN (GENERIC_PLAN) never does.

SourcesQ2 2027 SampleSource abstracts where samples come from, not what a sample means

Make explicit what each observation means, so new sources can't be mixed into the same statistical test by accident.

Read moreShow less

internal/telemetry/promsource already requires a per-interval mean, but nothing in the interface enforces it, and a future histogram- or percentile-based source would be indistinguishable from a mean-based one to the engine. Making the meaning of each observation explicit (interval mean, cumulative mean, histogram-derived, gauge) in the sample type — with a single normalisation step in front of the engine rather than per-source conventions — would keep the engine independent of the ingestion protocol. Percentile (p95/p99) detection needs its own statistical path and calibration; feeding percentiles through the mean-based Welch test is not an option.

IntegrationsQ2 2027 OLM bundle for OperatorHub.io

An OLM bundle for OperatorHub.io.

Plan-diffUnscheduled Real auto_explain log ingestion is not yet built

A log-shipping pipeline for clusters that have neither pg_store_plans nor PostgreSQL 16.

Read moreShow less

internal/planner captures a query's execution plan from either pg_store_plans (the real, previously-executed plan — see Testing for how it's validated against a real install) or EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON, GENERIC_PLAN) (an estimate, PostgreSQL 16+ only) and diffs two captures — see Detection Algorithm. A full auto_explain log-shipping pipeline remains a heavier, not-yet-started alternative for clusters that have neither pg_store_plans nor PostgreSQL 16 available — see the "Honest limitations" note on Detection Algorithm.

StatisticsUnscheduled Block bootstrap and adaptive baselines

Better significance for autocorrelated series, and baselines that adapt over time.

Read moreShow less

Block-permutation or block-bootstrap significance for autocorrelated series, and adaptive baseline models.

StatisticsUnscheduled Histogram and tail-latency detection

Detect regressions in the tail of the distribution, not only in the mean.

Read moreShow less

Histogram and tail-latency change detection.

AttributionUnscheduled Traces as attribution evidence

Traces add context and execution paths to an attribution; they don't prove one.

Read moreShow less

Using OpenTelemetry traces as extra attribution evidence (which service, endpoint, and application version was affected). Traces give context and execution paths, not a counterfactual, so they should inform an attribution result rather than prove one.

AttributionUnscheduled Control groups and causal methods

Compare against control queries and history to estimate calibrated attribution probabilities.

Read moreShow less

Control-group methods (difference-in-differences against comparable queries), counterfactual baselines from history, and empirically calibrated attribution probabilities.

docs.title: Config and Secrets
docs.text: How to store the Postgres DSN in a Secret, what the consent label does, and how to rotate a credential.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The radar needs one credential above all: the connection string (DSN) for the Postgres it watches. It may also hold a webhook token, alert destinations and an OTLP header. Kubernetes has two objects for this kind of data, ConfigMaps and Secrets. This page explains the difference, how a pod receives either, and the exact steps to give the radar its DSN safely.

docs.title: ConfigMaps and Secrets
docs.text:
Both are objects holding key/value pairs that live outside the container image. A ConfigMap is for non-sensitive settings; a Secret is for credentials and tokens. They are used the same way, but the cluster treats Secrets more carefully: their values are hidden from kubectl describe, access to them is a separate RBAC permission, and they can be encrypted at rest if the cluster is configured for it.

Base64 is not encryption

Values in a Secret are stored base64-encoded, which is only a text encoding. Anyone who can kubectl get secret -o yaml can read the plaintext. The protection of a Secret is who is allowed to read it, not how it looks. Keep Secret read access narrow, and never commit a Secret manifest with real values to git.

kubectl get secrets -n <ns>
kubectl get secret postgres-credentials -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.data.dsn}' | base64 -d

docs.title: How a pod receives them
docs.text:
A pod gets Secret and ConfigMap values in one of two ways:

Way What it looks like When values update Environment variable from a key env: [{name: POSTGRES_DSN, valueFrom: {secretKeyRef: {name: ..., key: dsn}}}] only when the pod restarts Mounted as a file a volume appears as files in a directory the file updates in place, after a delay

The radar's operator mode takes its Secret values as environment variables (POSTGRES_DSN, SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL, and so on, filled from the chart's Secret). This has one consequence you must remember: changing a Secret does not change a running pod's environment. After you update a Secret that operator mode reads, restart it:

kubectl rollout restart deployment/<fullname> -n <ns>
kubectl rollout status deployment/<fullname> -n <ns>

manager mode is different: it reads the Secret through the Kubernetes API when it reconciles a PostgresWatch (the dsnSecretRef field), so it does not depend on the pod's environment for the DSN.

docs.title: Create the DSN Secret
docs.text:
The DSN is a standard PostgreSQL connection URL. Use a least-privilege role, never a superuser; the role setup is in Installation.

kubectl create secret generic orders-dsn -n <ns> \
  --from-literal=dsn='postgres://pgrr_monitor:change-me@orders-rw.<ns>.svc.cluster.local:5432/orders?sslmode=require'

Two details worth getting right:

  • Single-quote the value. Passwords containing $, ! or & are mangled by the shell inside double quotes.
  • Special characters in the password must be percent-encoded in the URL (@ becomes %40, / becomes %2F). A DSN that works in psql with a keyword string may fail as a URL for this reason.

Keep the password out of your shell history

--from-literal leaves the value in your shell history. Prefer --from-file=dsn=./dsn.txt with a file you delete afterwards, or create the Secret from your secret manager's tooling.

docs.title: Applying it from a manifest
docs.text:
If you manage Secrets as manifests, use stringData so you can write plain text and let Kubernetes encode it:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: orders-dsn
  namespace: <ns>
  labels:
    pg-regression-radar.io/allow-postgreswatch-access: "true"
type: Opaque
stringData:
  dsn: postgres://pgrr_monitor:change-me@orders-rw.<ns>.svc.cluster.local:5432/orders?sslmode=require

docs.title: The consent label
docs.text:
In manager mode the radar's ServiceAccount can read Secrets cluster-wide, so that it can resolve any PostgresWatch's dsnSecretRef. To stop that power being used on someone else's behalf, the radar refuses to use a Secret unless its owner has labelled it:

kubectl label secret orders-dsn -n <ns> \
  pg-regression-radar.io/allow-postgreswatch-access=true

Without that label the PostgresWatch ends up in status.phase: Failed, with the reason in status.message:

kubectl get postgreswatch orders -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.status.phase}{"\n"}{.status.message}{"\n"}'

Labelling a Secret needs the same permission as editing it, so only the people who own the Secret can opt it in. The reasoning, and the admission policies that restrict who may set the label in shared clusters, are in RBAC and access.

In pg-regression-radar

The Helm chart creates its own Secret, <fullname>-secret, with the consent label already set, holding the keys dsn, slackWebhookUrl, alertUrl, stateDsn, and, only when you set them, pagerDutyRoutingKey, alertTemplate, otlpHeaders and webhookSecret. If you create a PostgresWatch yourself, the Secret and its label are yours to create.

docs.title: Pointing a PostgresWatch at the Secret
docs.text:
apiVersion: radar.pgregressionradar.io/v1alpha1
kind: PostgresWatch
metadata:
  name: orders
  namespace: <ns>
spec:
  clusterName: orders
  dsnSecretRef:
    name: orders-dsn      # the Secret's name, in the SAME namespace
    key: dsn              # the key inside it

The Secret must be in the PostgresWatch's own namespace (see Objects and namespaces). Prefer dsnSecretRef over putting the DSN directly in the spec: a plain DSN in a PostgresWatch shows up in kubectl get postgreswatch -o yaml and in anyone's describe output.

docs.title: Rotating a credential
docs.text:
1. Change the password in Postgres (or create the new role).
  2. Update the Secret: kubectl create secret generic orders-dsn -n <ns> --from-literal=dsn='...' --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -.
  3. operator mode: kubectl rollout restart deployment/<fullname> -n <ns>. manager mode: nothing to restart. The manager re-reads the Secret on every reconcile (about every 30 seconds for a running watch) and, because the DSN is part of what it compares, restarts that watch's worker on its own when the credential changed.

The pipe in step 2 is the standard way to update a Secret from literals: create --dry-run=client -o yaml renders the manifest and apply applies it, so it works whether or not the Secret exists.

docs.title: Webhook authentication
docs.text: If you protect the deploy-event endpoint with a token, the sender must send it in an X-Webhook-Token header, and the radar compares it with the configured secret. With the chart, set ingester.webhookSecret; it lands in the chart's Secret under webhookSecret. Leaving it empty leaves POST /webhook open to anyone who can reach the Service, which is acceptable only while the Service stays cluster-internal. See Deploy Sources & Webhooks.

docs.title: CRDs and operators
docs.text: How PostgresWatch and the other radar kinds exist, what the controller does, and the install rules.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Kubernetes ships with kinds like Pod and Deployment. A CustomResourceDefinition (CRD) teaches the API server a new kind, and a controller (often called an operator when it manages an application) is a program that watches objects of that kind and acts on them. The radar's manager mode is exactly this: four CRDs plus one controller deployment. Knowing how the two halves relate answers most install and upgrade questions before they come up.

docs.title: CRD, custom resource, controller
docs.text:
Three separate things, easy to conflate:

Thing What it is Example CRD the definition of a kind: its name, fields and validation. Installed once per cluster. postgreswatches.radar.pgregressionradar.io Custom resource (CR) an instance of that kind, written by you a PostgresWatch named orders Controller a running program that watches CRs and makes reality match them the radar's manager Deployment

Without the CRD, the API server rejects your YAML. Without the controller, your CRs are accepted and stored, and nothing happens: they just sit there with no status. A PostgresWatch with an empty Phase column usually means the controller is not running.

docs.title: The reconcile loop
docs.text:
A controller does one thing, repeatedly:

  1. Observe the desired state (the CR's spec) and the actual state.
  2. Act to close the gap.
  3. Report the outcome in the CR's status.

The controller does not run once per kubectl apply; it runs whenever the CR changes, whenever something it depends on changes (the DSN Secret, the Deployment it watches) and periodically. This is why Kubernetes setups are described as eventually consistent: you edit the spec, and status catches up a moment later.

kubectl apply -f my-watch.yaml
kubectl get postgreswatch orders -n <ns> -w        # watch the phase move from Pending to Running

In pg-regression-radar

The manager runs one reconcile loop per kind. For each PostgresWatch it starts a scrape and detection worker; for each DeploySource it registers a route or a workload watch; for each detection it creates a PerformanceRegression. If the manager restarts, it re-reads the CRs and starts everything again, which is why your configuration lives in objects and not in the pod.

docs.title: The four radar kinds
docs.text:
Kind Short name Scope You write it? What it is PostgresWatch pgw namespaced yes one Postgres cluster to watch, with detection and alerting settings DeploySource pgds namespaced yes where deploy events come from, tied to one PostgresWatch PerformanceRegression pgreg namespaced no (the radar creates it) one detection result, with the query, latency change and plan diff PostgresRadarCluster pgrc cluster admins a registered remote cluster, for multi-cluster mode

All four belong to the API group radar.pgregressionradar.io, version v1alpha1. The alpha in the version means the schema can still change between releases; see API Versioning for what is promised.

Short names make the daily commands shorter:

kubectl get pgw,pgds -n <ns>           # PostgresWatch and DeploySource
kubectl get pgreg -n <ns>              # PerformanceRegression
kubectl get pgreg -A                   # across every namespace
kubectl get pgrc                       # PostgresRadarCluster (cluster-scoped, no -n)

docs.title: Reading the columns
docs.text:
The CRDs define the columns kubectl get shows, so the table is a status summary on its own:

Kind Columns What to look for PostgresWatch Cluster, Phase, tracked queries, Age Phase should be Running. Pending or Failed has a reason in status.message. DeploySource Watch, Source, Phase, Webhook path, Age Phase is Ready when the route (or watch) is active; Pending until its PostgresWatch exists. PerformanceRegression Watch, Query, Status, Confidence, P value, Latency change, Age Status is Detected, NoRegression or InsufficientData.

For the full picture of one object, kubectl describe (events and conditions) and -o yaml (every field):

kubectl describe postgreswatch orders -n <ns>
kubectl get pgreg -n <ns> -o yaml | less

docs.title: Discovering the schema
docs.text:
You do not need the docs open to write a CR. The schema is in the cluster:

kubectl explain postgreswatch                         # top-level fields
kubectl explain postgreswatch.spec                    # everything under spec
kubectl explain postgreswatch.spec.alerting           # a nested block
kubectl explain deploysource.spec.sourceType

The reference tables for every field are in the Configuration Reference; explain is the quick check while you edit.

docs.title: status, phases and conditions
docs.text:
CRs separate spec and status through the status subresource: the controller updates status with its own permissions, and an edit to spec does not wipe it. Two patterns you will see:

  • status.phase (and status.message): a short state and, on failure, the reason. Read it as the first thing: 
    kubectl get postgreswatch orders -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.status.phase}{"  "}{.status.message}{"\n"}'
  • status.conditions: a list of type/status/reason/message entries, the standard Kubernetes way to report several independent facts. kubectl describe prints them in a readable table.

docs.title: Installing and upgrading the definitions
docs.text:
The CRDs must exist before any CR is created, and they must be Established (accepted by the API server) a moment after applying. Two rules cover nearly every problem:

1. Wait for Established before creating CRs. Applying CRDs and CRs in the same command can fail with no matches for kind, because the API server needs a moment to start serving the new kind:

kubectl apply -f crds/
kubectl wait --for=condition=Established --timeout=60s \
  crd/postgreswatches.radar.pgregressionradar.io \
  crd/deploysources.radar.pgregressionradar.io \
  crd/performanceregressions.radar.pgregressionradar.io
kubectl apply -f my-watch.yaml

2. Helm installs CRDs on install only, never on upgrade. This is deliberate Helm behaviour: CRDs are cluster-wide and removing or changing them can destroy data, so Helm does not touch them after the first install. To pick up a schema change from a newer chart, apply the files yourself:

kubectl apply -f deploy/helm/deploylens/crds/

Deleting a CRD deletes every object of that kind

kubectl delete crd postgreswatches.radar.pgregressionradar.io removes all PostgresWatch objects in every namespace, instantly. helm uninstall leaves CRDs in place for exactly this reason. Remove them only on purpose, and export what you want to keep first: kubectl get pgreg -A -o yaml > regressions-backup.yaml.

docs.title: Finalizers, in one paragraph
docs.text: Some objects will not disappear on kubectl delete: they sit in Terminating. That is usually a finalizer (an entry in metadata.finalizers) telling Kubernetes "wait until a controller has cleaned up". If the controller is gone, the object waits forever. Bring the controller back, and the deletion completes. Removing finalizers by hand is a last resort that skips the cleanup.

docs.title: Leader election and the Lease
docs.text:
When you run several manager replicas, they coordinate through a Lease object (API group coordination.k8s.io) in the manager's namespace. Whoever holds the lease is the leader and does all the work; the rest stand by. If the leader stops renewing, another replica takes the lease. You can see it:

kubectl get lease -n <ns>

More on what this means for logs in Pods and Deployments.

docs.title: Helm basics
docs.text: Charts, releases and values, and the Helm commands to install, inspect, upgrade and remove the radar.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes and the supported way to install the radar. A chart is a bundle of templated manifests; a release is one installation of a chart in a cluster; values are the settings you give it. Instead of writing a dozen manifests by hand, you set a few values and Helm renders and applies the whole set. This page covers the vocabulary and the commands that matter, and the details specific to this chart.

docs.title: Vocabulary
docs.text:
Term Meaning In this project Chart a directory (or OCI artifact) of templates plus default values.yaml deploy/helm/deploylens, or oci://ghcr.io/joao00001/charts/pg-regression-radar Release a named installation of a chart in a namespace whatever name you pass to helm install; objects are named from it Values settings that fill the templates mode, postgres.dsn, alerting.*, manager.replicaCount, ... Revision a numbered version of a release, created on every install, upgrade and rollback helm history lists them

The release name matters because it ends up in object names. The chart builds <fullname> from the release name, adding the chart name unless the release name already contains it, so helm install radar ... gives objects like radar-deploylens-manager. kubectl get deploy -n <ns> shows the real names.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
helm install radar oci://ghcr.io/joao00001/charts/pg-regression-radar \
  --version <version> \
  --namespace <ns> --create-namespace \
  --set mode=manager \
  --set postgres.dsn='postgres://pgrr_monitor:change-me@orders-rw.<ns>.svc.cluster.local:5432/orders?sslmode=require' \
  --set postgres.clusterName=orders
Part Meaning radar the release name oci://... the chart. An OCI registry needs no helm repo add. A local clone works too: ./deploy/helm/deploylens. --version the chart's SemVer, which is the release tag without the leading v (Installation) --namespace, --create-namespace where the release lives; create it if it does not exist --set key=value one value, from the command line

Unlike kubectl apply, helm install fails if the release name already exists in that namespace. To install or upgrade with one command, use helm upgrade --install.

docs.title: Values: --set versus a file
docs.text:
For more than two or three settings, put them in a file:

# my-values.yaml
mode: manager
postgres:
  clusterName: orders
  scrapeIntervalSeconds: 60
manager:
  replicaCount: 2
alerting:
  slackWebhookUrl: https://hooks.slack.com/services/XXX/YYY/ZZZ

helm upgrade --install radar oci://ghcr.io/joao00001/charts/pg-regression-radar \
  --version <version> -n <ns> --create-namespace -f my-values.yaml \
  --set postgres.dsn="$PGRR_DSN"          # keep secrets out of the file

Values from later -f files and from --set override earlier ones, and everything you do not set keeps the chart's default. To see every value the chart accepts, with comments:

helm show values oci://ghcr.io/joao00001/charts/pg-regression-radar --version <version>

Values you pass on the command line are stored in the release

Helm stores the merged values in a Secret in the cluster (sh.helm.release.v1...) so it can roll back. Anyone who can read Secrets in that namespace can read your DSN from it. This is one more reason to keep Secret access narrow, and why the chart's own Secret, <fullname>-secret, is what the pods actually read.

docs.title: See what you would apply: template
docs.text:
helm template renders the manifests locally and prints them. It changes nothing, and it is the cheapest way to check a values file before you apply it:

helm template radar ./deploy/helm/deploylens -f my-values.yaml | less
helm template radar ./deploy/helm/deploylens -f my-values.yaml | kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f -
helm lint ./deploy/helm/deploylens -f my-values.yaml

The --dry-run=server variant sends the rendered manifests to the API server for validation without creating anything.

docs.title: Inspect a running release
docs.text:
helm list -n <ns>                      # releases and their status
helm status radar -n <ns>              # status, plus the chart's own NOTES
helm get values radar -n <ns>          # the values YOU set
helm get values radar -n <ns> --all    # the merged values, defaults included
helm get manifest radar -n <ns>        # the objects Helm applied
helm history radar -n <ns>             # revisions

helm get values is the first command to run when someone asks "how is this installed?" It answers without guessing.

docs.title: Upgrade and roll back
docs.text:
helm upgrade radar oci://ghcr.io/joao00001/charts/pg-regression-radar \
  --version <new-version> -n <ns> --reuse-values
helm rollback radar 3 -n <ns>          # back to revision 3

Two details are easy to get wrong:

  • --reuse-values versus -f. --reuse-values keeps the values from the last release and ignores new defaults in the chart, which can hide new options. Passing your -f my-values.yaml every time is more predictable: your file is the source of truth.
  • Rollback restores the release's objects, not the CRDs. See the next section.

The chart's image.tag defaults to the chart's own appVersion, so upgrading the chart upgrades the radar image with it, unless you pinned a tag.

docs.title: CRDs and Helm
docs.text:
Helm applies the chart's crds/ directory only on helm install. It never updates or deletes it. That is deliberate Helm behaviour, because CRDs are cluster-wide and changing them can affect every object of that kind. Three consequences for the radar:

  • After helm upgrade to a chart with a changed CRD schema, apply the new definitions yourself: kubectl apply -f deploy/helm/deploylens/crds/.
  • helm uninstall leaves the CRDs, and therefore your PerformanceRegression history, in the cluster.
  • In operator mode, no CRDs are used at all.

See CRDs and operators.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
helm uninstall radar -n <ns>

This removes everything the release created: the Deployment, Service, Secret, ServiceAccount and RBAC objects. It does not remove the namespace you created, and it does not remove the CRDs or the custom resources you created yourself (including any PostgresWatch you applied separately).

docs.title: Mode and the objects it creates
docs.text:
The single most important value is mode. It decides what Helm creates:

mode Creates Notable operator (default) a Deployment, a Service, a ServiceAccount, the Secret configured by flags and environment; no CRDs, no cluster-scoped objects manager a Deployment (manager.replicaCount, default 2), a Service, ServiceAccount, ClusterRole and binding, a leader-election Role, the CRDs, the Secret, and unless manager.createDefaultWatch=false, a PostgresWatch and a DeploySource production mode; see Architecture Overview

Optional guard rails (networkPolicy.enabled, resourceQuota.enabled, limitRange.enabled) are off by default and described in Hardening (Helm).

docs.title: Troubleshooting Helm itself
docs.text: Message Meaning and fix cannot re-use a name that is still in use a release with that name exists. Use helm upgrade --install, or pick another name. Kubernetes cluster unreachable kubectl has no working context; check kubectl config current-context. rendered manifests contain a resource that already exists an object of the same name exists that Helm does not own, often left from a manual kubectl apply. Delete it or rename the release. no matches for kind "PostgresWatch" the CRDs are not installed (Helm skips crds/ on upgrade). Apply them, then retry. UPGRADE FAILED: another operation is in progress an earlier Helm command was interrupted. helm history shows a pending-* state; helm rollback to the last good revision.

docs.title: Services and networking
docs.text: How a webhook sender reaches the radar, how the radar reaches Postgres, and how to test from your laptop.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Pod IPs change every time a pod is replaced, so nothing in Kubernetes talks to a pod IP directly. Instead, traffic goes to a Service, a stable name and virtual IP that forwards to whichever pods currently match it. For the radar there are two connections to get right: Postgres to radar (the radar opens a connection to your database) and deploy sender to radar (ArgoCD, Flux, a CI job or an OpenTelemetry Collector posts events to the radar). This page covers both, plus kubectl port-forward for testing and NetworkPolicy for locking it down.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
A Service has a selector (which pods it targets, by label), ports and a type:

Type Reachable from Use ClusterIP (default) inside the cluster only everything the radar exposes, by default NodePort every node's IP on a high port quick tests on bare clusters LoadBalancer outside, through a cloud load balancer exposing the webhook beyond the cluster 
kubectl get service -n <ns>
kubectl describe service <fullname>-manager -n <ns>     # check the Endpoints line
kubectl get endpoints <fullname>-manager -n <ns>        # which pod IPs are behind it

Empty endpoints means the selector matches nothing

If Endpoints is <none>, the Service exists but sends traffic nowhere: either no pod matches its selector (a label mismatch) or no matching pod is Ready. This is the first thing to check when "the webhook times out".

docs.title: What the radar exposes
docs.text:
In manager mode, the Service <fullname>-manager has three ports:

Port name Default What it serves webhook 8080 deploy events: one route per DeploySource, at /webhook/<namespace>/<name> pg-metrics 9090 Prometheus metrics derived from pg_stat_statements ctrl-metrics 8443 controller-runtime's own reconcile and queue metrics

The health probes (8081) are not on the Service: the kubelet probes the pod directly. In operator mode, the Service <fullname> exposes webhook and metrics on service.webhookPort and service.metricsPort. The chart's default service.type is ClusterIP.

docs.title: DNS: how names resolve
docs.text:
Every Service gets a DNS name inside the cluster:

<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local

Within the same namespace the short name <service> is enough; from another namespace use <service>.<namespace>. The full form always works.

This is how you tell things where the radar is:

# a deploy sender in any namespace posting to the radar
http://<fullname>-manager.<ns>.svc.cluster.local:8080/webhook/<ns>/<deploysource-name>

# the radar's DSN pointing at a Postgres Service
postgres://pgrr_monitor:...@orders-rw.<ns>.svc.cluster.local:5432/orders

For CloudNativePG, the read-write endpoint is the Service named <cluster>-rw (and -ro, -r for replicas). Point the DSN at -rw for the primary, which is where pg_stat_statements lives that you want to watch.

In pg-regression-radar

A DeploySource creates a route in the manager; its path is reported in status.webhookPath: kubectl get deploysource <name> -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.status.webhookPath}'. A DeploySource with sourceType: kubernetes has no webhook path, because the radar watches the workload itself and nothing needs to call it. Setting up senders is covered in Deploy Sources & Webhooks.

docs.title: Testing from your laptop: port-forward
docs.text:
A ClusterIP Service is not reachable from your machine. kubectl port-forward opens a temporary tunnel through the API server:

# in one terminal: forward local port 8080 to the manager Service
kubectl port-forward -n <ns> service/<fullname>-manager 8080:8080

# in another: post a test deploy event
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/webhook/<ns>/<deploysource-name> \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"app":"orders-api","namespace":"<ns>","revision":"abc123","timestamp":"2026-11-11T12:00:00Z"}'

Port-forward lasts only while the command runs, binds to localhost by default, and is for debugging, not for production access. The same works for metrics:

kubectl port-forward -n <ns> service/<fullname>-manager 9090:9090
curl -s localhost:9090/metrics | head

That payload matches a DeploySource with sourceType: generic; other source types expect their own payload shape (see Deploy Sources & Webhooks). If the request is refused with 401, the radar has a webhook secret configured: send it as -H 'X-Webhook-Token: <value>'. See Config and Secrets.

docs.title: Reaching the radar from outside the cluster
docs.text:
Only expose the webhook endpoint when a sender outside the cluster needs it, and always set a webhook secret first. Two common routes:

  • An Ingress (or Gateway) in front of the Service, with TLS. The Ingress controller is cluster-specific; the radar needs nothing special from it other than forwarding the path to port 8080.
  • A LoadBalancer Service (--set service.type=LoadBalancer), which is simpler but exposes the port directly.

Either way the endpoint must be authenticated, because an open endpoint lets anyone inject deploy events and skew detection. The chart prints a warning on install when ingester.webhookSecret is empty.

docs.title: NetworkPolicy
docs.text:
By default, any pod in a cluster can talk to any other pod. A NetworkPolicy restricts that: it selects pods by label and lists which ingress (incoming) and egress (outgoing) connections are allowed. Once any policy selects a pod for a direction, everything not listed for that direction is denied.

Two things you must know first:

  • Policies only work if your cluster's network plugin enforces them. On a cluster whose CNI does not, the objects are accepted and silently ignored.
  • The model is "default deny plus explicit allows". An empty policy that selects the radar's pods and lists no rules blocks all traffic to and from them. That is the right starting point, and it is also why a freshly applied policy "breaks" things until the allows are in.

The chart can render both parts for you (off by default):

helm upgrade --install radar deploy/helm/deploylens \
  --set mode=manager \
  --set networkPolicy.enabled=true \
  --set networkPolicy.egress.postgresCIDRs[0]=10.10.0.0/16 \
  --set networkPolicy.egress.apiServerCIDRs[0]=10.20.0.0/16

What the radar needs to be allowed, by direction:

Direction To / from Port Needed for ingress your deploy senders, Prometheus 8080, 9090 webhooks and metrics egress Postgres 5432 scraping pg_stat_statements egress the Kubernetes API server (manager mode only) 443 / 6443 reconciling objects, leader election egress cluster DNS 53 UDP/TCP resolving every name above egress your alert destination 443 Slack, PagerDuty, relay

The most frequent mistake is forgetting DNS and the API server egress. A manager that cannot resolve names or reach the API server fails in ways that look unrelated to the network. The full options, and how to adjust the DNS namespace, are in Hardening (Helm).

kubectl get networkpolicy -n <ns>
kubectl describe networkpolicy <fullname>-manager-allow -n <ns>

docs.title: Objects and namespaces
docs.text: Objects, namespaces and labels, and the kubectl commands you will use every day.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Kubernetes has one idea underneath everything: you declare the state you want as an object, and controllers continuously work to make reality match it. A Deployment, a Secret, a Service and the radar's own PostgresWatch are all objects, and they all follow the same shape. Once that shape is familiar, so is every command in the rest of this section.

docs.title: The shape of an object
docs.text:
Every object has the same four top-level fields:

apiVersion: radar.pgregressionradar.io/v1alpha1   # which API group and version defines this kind
kind: PostgresWatch                                # the type of object
metadata:                                          # identity: name, namespace, labels, annotations
  name: orders
  namespace: pgrr-lab
spec:                                              # what YOU want (desired state)
  clusterName: orders
  dsnSecretRef:
    name: postgres-credentials
    key: dsn
status:                                            # what IS (observed state), written by a controller
  phase: Running

Two rules matter more than any other:

  • You write spec; a controller writes status. Do not edit status by hand. When you want to know whether the radar accepted your PostgresWatch, you read its status.
  • apiVersion + kind + metadata.name + metadata.namespace identify the object. Applying the same YAML twice updates the object instead of creating a second one.

In pg-regression-radar

The things you write are PostgresWatch (what database to watch and how sensitively) and DeploySource (where deploy events come from). The things the radar writes are status on both of those, and whole PerformanceRegression objects, one per detection. See CRDs and operators.

docs.title: Namespaces
docs.text:
A namespace is a named partition of a cluster. Most objects live in exactly one namespace, and two objects of the same kind can share a name only if they are in different namespaces. Namespaces are how teams, environments and tools share a cluster without colliding.

kubectl get namespaces
kubectl create namespace pgrr-lab
kubectl get pods -n pgrr-lab        # one namespace
kubectl get pods -A                 # all namespaces

Some objects are cluster-scoped and belong to no namespace: nodes, CustomResourceDefinitions, ClusterRoles, and the radar's PostgresRadarCluster. You find out which is which with:

kubectl api-resources --namespaced=true
kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false

docs.title: Why namespaces matter for the radar
docs.text:
References between the radar's objects are by name, within a namespace. That is a rule you will trip on once if you do not know it:

Reference Where it is looked up DeploySource.spec.postgresWatchRef the PostgresWatch of that name in the same namespace as the DeploySource PostgresWatch.spec.dsnSecretRef the Secret of that name in the same namespace as the PostgresWatch (unless you use a remote cluster) DeploySource with sourceType: kubernetes, appName the Deployment or StatefulSet of that name in the same namespace as the DeploySource

So the radar and the app you are watching can live in different namespaces, but the PostgresWatch, its DeploySource and the Secret holding the DSN are created together in one namespace, and a kubernetes deploy source watches workloads in that same namespace.

Set the namespace once

Typing -n <ns> on every command gets old. Pin it for your current context instead: kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=<ns>. Check what you are pinned to with kubectl config view --minify | grep namespace.

docs.title: Labels, selectors and annotations
docs.text:
Labels are key/value pairs on an object's metadata that Kubernetes uses to select things. Annotations are key/value pairs that carry information but are never used for selection.

metadata:
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: orders-api
    app.kubernetes.io/component: api
  annotations:
    deployment.kubernetes.io/revision: "2"

A selector matches labels. A Service sends traffic to the pods whose labels match its selector; a Deployment manages the pods whose labels match its selector. That is the only glue between those objects, so a typo in a label is a silent failure: the Service exists and routes to nothing.

kubectl get pods -n <ns> --show-labels
kubectl get pods -n <ns> -l app.kubernetes.io/component=manager
kubectl label secret my-dsn -n <ns> some-key=some-value
kubectl label secret my-dsn -n <ns> some-key-          # trailing dash removes it

docs.title: Two metadata fields the radar relies on
docs.text:
• The consent label. pg-regression-radar.io/allow-postgreswatch-access: "true" on a Secret says "the owner of this Secret agrees that a PostgresWatch may read it". The radar refuses to use a Secret without it. The full reasoning is in RBAC and access; the how-to is in Config and Secrets.
  • The revision annotation. For a Deployment, deployment.kubernetes.io/revision is a counter Kubernetes bumps on every rollout. A DeploySource with sourceType: kubernetes uses it as the deploy's revision. See Pods and Deployments.

The Helm chart also puts the conventional app.kubernetes.io/name, app.kubernetes.io/instance and app.kubernetes.io/component labels on everything it creates, which is why -l app.kubernetes.io/component=manager selects the manager's objects.

docs.title: The kubectl commands you will use
docs.text:
You want to Command List objects of a kind kubectl get <kind> -n <ns> Watch a list change live kubectl get <kind> -n <ns> -w See one object in full, as stored kubectl get <kind> <name> -n <ns> -o yaml See an object plus its recent events kubectl describe <kind> <name> -n <ns> Pull one field out kubectl get <kind> <name> -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.status.phase}' Learn what fields a kind accepts kubectl explain postgreswatch.spec Create or update from a file kubectl apply -f file.yaml Delete kubectl delete -f file.yaml or kubectl delete <kind> <name> -n <ns> Read a pod's logs kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> (see Troubleshooting toolkit)

Three of these deserve a second look:

  • describe vs get -o yaml. get -o yaml is the raw object; describe is a human summary that also lists Events, the short log Kubernetes keeps about what happened to the object. When something is stuck, describe is usually the first thing to run.
  • explain works for the radar's kinds too, because their schemas are published in the cluster: kubectl explain postgreswatch.spec.alerting shows every field and its description without leaving the terminal.
  • -o jsonpath is how you script against status, for example waiting for a watch to be ready: kubectl get postgreswatch orders -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.status.phase}'.

docs.title: apply, not create
docs.text:
kubectl create -f file.yaml fails if the object exists. kubectl apply -f file.yaml creates it if it does not and updates it if it does, which is what lets you edit a manifest and re-apply it. Every manifest in this documentation is meant for apply.

kubectl apply -f my-watch.yaml
# edit my-watch.yaml
kubectl apply -f my-watch.yaml     # updates the same PostgresWatch in place

kubectl apply also accepts a URL or a directory, and a file with several objects separated by ---, which is how the lab installs its whole stack in one command.

docs.title: Order matters for custom resources
docs.text:
Objects of a custom kind (like PostgresWatch) can only be created after their definition exists in the cluster. That is why the lab waits for the CRDs between steps:

kubectl wait --for=condition=Established --timeout=60s \
  crd/postgreswatches.radar.pgregressionradar.io

If you ever see no matches for kind "PostgresWatch" in version "radar.pgregressionradar.io/v1alpha1", the definition is not installed yet. CRDs and operators explains why.

docs.title: Kubernetes basics
docs.text: The Kubernetes you need to install, operate and debug pg-regression-radar, and nothing more.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
pg-regression-radar is built to run in Kubernetes, and its manager mode is driven by Kubernetes objects: you describe what to watch in YAML, and the radar does the rest. You do not need to be a Kubernetes administrator to use it, but you do need a working model of a handful of concepts: objects and namespaces, Deployments, Secrets, Services, custom resources, RBAC and Helm. This section teaches exactly those, always from the point of view of what the radar does with each one.

Every page follows the same shape: the concept in a few paragraphs, the kubectl commands you will actually type, and a short "In pg-regression-radar" part that ties it back to the tool.

What this section does not cover

Building or sizing a cluster, choosing a CNI or a storage class, autoscaling, service meshes, GitOps tooling and Postgres operators (CloudNativePG and friends) are out of scope. If you can already run kubectl get pods against a cluster you are allowed to use, you have everything this section assumes.

docs.title: What you need on your machine
docs.text:
Tool Needed for Check kubectl everything on these pages kubectl version --client helm (3.x) only the Helm install path (Helm basics) helm version A cluster and a kubeconfig a place to run the radar: kind, minikube, k3d, Docker Desktop, or a real cluster kubectl config current-context

kubectl talks to whichever cluster your current context points at. Before running anything that changes state, confirm you are where you think you are:

kubectl config current-context
kubectl config get-contexts
kubectl get nodes

Check the context before you apply

The most common Kubernetes mistake is applying a manifest to the wrong cluster. kubectl apply does not ask for confirmation. If you work with more than one cluster, make kubectl config current-context a habit before every install or delete.

docs.title: What permissions you need
docs.text:
Installing the radar in manager mode creates cluster-scoped objects (CustomResourceDefinitions, a ClusterRole and a ClusterRoleBinding), so the person installing it needs cluster-level rights. You can check before you start:

kubectl auth can-i create customresourcedefinitions
kubectl auth can-i create clusterroles
kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n <ns>

operator mode creates nothing cluster-scoped: a Deployment, a Service, a ServiceAccount and a Secret in one namespace are enough. See RBAC and access for what each mode asks for.

docs.text:

  • You are installing it for real, in manager mode: read all of them in order. The pages build on each other, and RBAC and access explains the one security decision you have to make (the consent label).
  • You run it in operator mode: Config and Secrets, Services and networking and Helm basics cover almost everything; the CRD pages are background.
  • Something is broken: go straight to Troubleshooting toolkit.

docs.title: Conventions on these pages
docs.text:
• <ns> stands for the namespace the radar is installed in. In the lab it is pgrr-lab.
  • <fullname> stands for the name Helm gives the chart's objects: the release name, plus the chart name unless the release name already contains it. Find the real value with kubectl get deploy -n <ns>.
  • Commands that only read are shown plain. Commands that change something say so in the text around them.
  • Every command works with a plain kubectl; none of them needs a plugin.

docs.title: A ten-minute look at a running install
docs.text:
If the radar is already running (the lab is the easiest way to get one), these four commands show you most of what the rest of the section explains:

# 1. The radar's pods. Look for READY 1/1 and STATUS Running.
kubectl get pods -n <ns>

# 2. The things you configure, in one call (short names, see "CRDs and operators").
kubectl get postgreswatch,deploysource -n <ns>

# 3. The things the radar produces.
kubectl get performanceregressions -n <ns>

# 4. What the radar says about itself.
kubectl logs -n <ns> deployment/<fullname>-manager --tail=50

If any of these shows something you do not recognise, the page for that concept is in the table above.

docs.title: RBAC and access
docs.text: What permissions the radar asks for and why, how to check them, and the consent label for Secrets.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Kubernetes decides every request with RBAC (role-based access control): a subject (a user or a ServiceAccount) is granted verbs (get, list, create, ...) on resources (pods, secrets, postgreswatches, ...), cluster-wide or inside one namespace. The radar's manager is a program calling the Kubernetes API, so it has a ServiceAccount with a role, and that role is the whole of its power. This page explains the objects involved, then walks through what the radar gets and why.

docs.title: The objects
docs.text:
Object What it is Scope ServiceAccount the identity a pod runs as when it calls the API namespaced Role a list of permissions (verbs on resources) one namespace ClusterRole the same, but cluster-wide, or for cluster-scoped resources cluster RoleBinding grants a Role (or ClusterRole) to subjects inside one namespace namespaced ClusterRoleBinding grants a ClusterRole to subjects across the whole cluster cluster

A role on its own does nothing; a binding is what attaches it to an identity. A rule looks like this:

rules:
  - apiGroups: ["apps"]                  # the API group ("" is the core group: pods, secrets, services)
    resources: ["deployments"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]      # read-only

The verbs that matter: get (one object), list and watch (many objects, and following changes), create, update, patch, delete. Controllers nearly always need get, list and watch together, because they keep a local cache fed by a watch.

docs.title: Testing permissions: kubectl auth can-i
docs.text:
You never have to guess what an identity can do:

kubectl auth can-i create customresourcedefinitions                      # you
kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n <ns>
kubectl auth can-i list deployments -A \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<serviceaccount>                       # the radar's ServiceAccount
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<serviceaccount> -n <ns>

The ServiceAccount's name is <fullname> unless you set serviceAccount.name; kubectl get serviceaccount -n <ns> shows it. --as needs permission to impersonate, which cluster admins have.

A refused request is reported as forbidden, with the exact verb, resource and identity in the message:

deployments.apps is forbidden: User "system:serviceaccount:radar:radar-deploylens"
cannot list resource "deployments" in API group "apps" at the cluster scope

That message is a complete diagnosis: that identity needs list on deployments in the apps group.

docs.title: What the radar's manager gets
docs.text:
The chart creates, in manager mode, a ServiceAccount, a ClusterRole with a ClusterRoleBinding, and a namespaced Role for leader election. Nothing in them can write to your workloads or read your Pods.

Permission Resources Why read postgreswatches, deploysources, postgresradarclusters to know what to do update status the /status of those kinds, and of performanceregressions to report phase and message read, create, update, patch performanceregressions to record each detection read deployments, statefulsets (apps) the kubernetes deploy source watches rollouts. It never writes to a workload. read secrets (core group) to resolve dsnSecretRef and other referenced Secrets read, create, update, delete leases (coordination.k8s.io), in the manager's namespace only leader election get, patch on rollouts argoproj.io, only if manager.autoAbort.rbacEnabled the optional auto-abort feature

Two things in that table are deliberate:

  • The cluster-wide Secret read. The manager must be able to read a Secret in any namespace where someone creates a PostgresWatch, so it cannot be limited to one namespace. That is a big power, and the next section is what stops it being abused.
  • Everything optional is off by default. Argo Rollouts access is granted only when you ask for it, so a cluster without it, or a team that never enables auto-abort, does not get the permission for nothing.
kubectl get clusterrole,clusterrolebinding | grep <fullname>
kubectl describe clusterrole <fullname>-manager-role

operator mode never talks to the Kubernetes API, so it needs none of this. You can even stop mounting a token in its pods with serviceAccount.automountServiceAccountToken=false (Hardening). Keep it true in manager mode.

docs.title: The administrator role
docs.text: The chart also creates a ClusterRole named <fullname>-cluster-registry-admin, which can fully manage PostgresRadarCluster objects (registrations of remote clusters). It is not bound to anyone. Bind it to your platform administrators, never to the manager's own ServiceAccount. See Multi-Cluster (Fleet) Mode.

docs.title: The consent label
docs.text:
The cluster-wide Secret read creates a classic problem, a confused deputy. Suppose a team has permission to create PostgresWatch objects in their namespace, but not to read Secrets there. They could write dsnSecretRef: {name: some-other-teams-secret} and have the manager, which can read it, use it on their behalf. The manager's power would be exercised at the request of someone who does not have it.

The fix is in the radar, not in RBAC. The manager refuses to use any Secret unless its owner has opted it in with a label:

kubectl label secret orders-dsn -n <ns> pg-regression-radar.io/allow-postgreswatch-access=true
  • If the label is missing, the PostgresWatch goes to status.phase: Failed, with the reason in status.message. It never reads the contents.
  • Setting the label needs the same permission as editing the Secret. So only someone who could already change the Secret can opt it in.
  • This applies to both dsnSecretRef and the kubeconfig Secret used for remote clusters.

In a single-team cluster this is a one-line step and no more thought is needed. In a shared cluster, treat the label as a privilege of its own: if tenants can edit their own Secrets, they can label them too, and a tenant who can both label a Secret and create a PostgresWatch can point the radar at anything they can write. The repo ships three ready-to-adapt policies for locking this down:

File What it is docs/policies/rbac-consent-labeler-example.yaml a dedicated ServiceAccount and role that are the only identities allowed to set the label docs/policies/validating-admission-policy-consent-label.yaml a built-in (CEL) ValidatingAdmissionPolicy rejecting the label from anyone else; needs no extra software docs/policies/kyverno-consent-label-policy.yaml the same rule as a Kyverno policy, if you already run Kyverno

The reasoning and the full threat model are in Security Model and Multi-Cluster (Fleet) Mode.

docs.title: Pod Security
docs.text:
Separate from RBAC, the cluster can restrict what a pod may do once it is allowed to exist: run as root, mount the host, add capabilities. Pod Security Admission does this with labels on the namespace:

kubectl label namespace <ns> \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted

The chart's defaults already satisfy the strictest level (restricted): non-root user, no privilege escalation, all capabilities dropped, a read-only root filesystem and the default seccomp profile. So you can enforce restricted on the radar's namespace without changing a value. See Hardening (Helm).

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: You see It means Fix forbidden in the manager's logs its role is missing a verb or resource kubectl auth can-i ... --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa>, then check the ClusterRole and its binding PostgresWatch in Failed, message mentions the label the Secret has no consent label label the Secret (above) Error from server (Forbidden) on your own kubectl apply your user lacks the permission, not the radar kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource> -n <ns> cannot create resource "customresourcedefinitions" on install CRDs are cluster-scoped and you are not a cluster admin ask an admin to install the CRDs once pods rejected with violates PodSecurity a namespace policy conflicts with an overridden security context remove the override or relax the namespace label
