docs.title: Troubleshooting toolkit
docs.text: A fixed order of checks, the commands for each, and a symptom-to-cause table for the radar.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Almost every problem with the radar is one of five things: a pod that is not running, a custom resource that is not accepted, a reference that does not resolve, a permission that is missing, or a connection that is blocked. Kubernetes tells you which, if you look in the right places in the right order. This page is that order, followed by the radar-specific symptoms.

docs.title: The order of checks
docs.text:
Work down this list and stop at the first thing that looks wrong. Each step costs one command.

  1. Is the radar running? kubectl get pods -n <ns>
  2. Did it accept my configuration? kubectl get pgw,pgds -n <ns>: look at Phase.
  3. What does it say? kubectl logs ...
  4. What does Kubernetes say about it? kubectl describe and events.
  5. Is a permission missing? kubectl auth can-i ... --as=...
  6. Is the network blocking it? kubectl get endpoints, port-forward, NetworkPolicy.

docs.title: 1. Is the radar running?
docs.text:
kubectl get pods -n <ns>
STATUS Meaning Next step Running, READY 1/1 healthy go to step 2 Running, READY 0/1 the readiness probe is failing kubectl describe pod, then logs Pending no node could take it, or a quota blocked it kubectl describe pod: read Events at the bottom ImagePullBackOff / ErrImagePull the node cannot fetch the image wrong tag, a private registry, or no internet. describe shows the exact error. CrashLoopBackOff the container starts and exits repeatedly kubectl logs <pod> --previous OOMKilled (in describe, under Last State) it exceeded its memory limit raise resources.limits.memory (manager.resources in manager mode) Completed a one-off pod finished normal for Jobs, not for the radar 
# The Events section at the bottom is usually the answer.
kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns>
kubectl get events -n <ns> --sort-by=.lastTimestamp

docs.title: 2. Did it accept my configuration?
docs.text:
kubectl get postgreswatch,deploysource -n <ns>
kubectl get postgreswatch <name> -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.status.phase}{"  "}{.status.message}{"\n"}'
kubectl describe postgreswatch <name> -n <ns>
Phase Meaning Running (watch), Ready (source) working Pending the controller has not got to it yet, or (for a DeploySource) its PostgresWatch does not exist in this namespace yet Failed the controller tried and could not. status.message is the reason. empty no controller has touched it: the manager is not running, or the CRD was applied but no manager is installed

status.message is usually specific: a Secret without the consent label, a Secret key that does not exist, a DSN that cannot connect, a remote cluster that is unreachable.

docs.title: 3. Logs
docs.text:
kubectl logs -n <ns> deployment/<fullname>-manager               # one pod, picked for you
kubectl logs -n <ns> <pod> --tail=100
kubectl logs -n <ns> <pod> --since=15m
kubectl logs -n <ns> <pod> -f                                     # follow
kubectl logs -n <ns> <pod> --previous       # the container that just crashed
# Every replica at once, each line prefixed with its pod.
kubectl logs -n <ns> -l app.kubernetes.io/component=manager --all-containers --prefix

Remember that with several manager replicas only the leader works (Pods and Deployments). The -l ... --prefix form reads all replicas at once, which finds the leader's log without guessing.

The radar's images are built on a distroless base, so there is no shell inside them: kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh will fail. That is expected. Everything you need is in the logs, the CR statuses and the metrics endpoint.

Most useful log lines are errors from the reconcilers

Look for unable to resolve DSN, unable to start watch worker and forbidden. Detection itself logs at a quieter level; a failing plan capture, for instance, is logged at DEBUG.

docs.title: 4. Events and describe
docs.text:
Events are Kubernetes' short-lived log of what happened to an object: scheduled, pulled, started, killed, failed a probe, rejected by a quota. They expire after about an hour, so look soon.

kubectl describe deployment <fullname>-manager -n <ns>
# Why a rollout is stuck: pod creation errors show up on the ReplicaSet.
kubectl describe replicaset -n <ns> -l app.kubernetes.io/component=manager
kubectl get events -n <ns> --field-selector type=Warning

If a Deployment says 0/2 ready and has no pods at all, look at its ReplicaSet's events: that is where exceeded quota and violates PodSecurity messages appear, because the ReplicaSet creates the pods.

docs.title: 5. Permissions
docs.text:
kubectl auth can-i list deployments.apps -A --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<serviceaccount>
kubectl logs -n <ns> deployment/<fullname>-manager | grep -i forbidden

A forbidden message names the identity, verb and resource exactly. See RBAC and access.

docs.title: 6. Network
docs.text:
# <none> means the Service selects no ready pod.
kubectl get endpoints <fullname>-manager -n <ns>
kubectl get networkpolicy -n <ns>                       # a policy can silently drop traffic
kubectl port-forward -n <ns> service/<fullname>-manager 8080:8080

If port-forward works but your sender cannot reach the Service, the problem is between the sender and the cluster, not the radar: a NetworkPolicy, a wrong DNS name, or a wrong port. See Services and networking.

docs.title: Symptoms specific to the radar
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Check or fix no matches for kind "PostgresWatch" on apply CRDs not installed yet, or not yet Established kubectl get crd \| grep radar; apply CRDs, then kubectl wait --for=condition=Established crd/postgreswatches.radar.pgregressionradar.io PostgresWatch Failed, message about the label the DSN Secret lacks the consent label kubectl label secret <name> -n <ns> pg-regression-radar.io/allow-postgreswatch-access=true PostgresWatch Failed, message about a key or Secret not found dsnSecretRef points at the wrong name or key, or the Secret is in another namespace kubectl get secret <name> -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.data}' and compare with name and key PostgresWatch Failed, DSN connection errors wrong host, password, SSL mode, or a NetworkPolicy blocking egress to Postgres check the DSN from a throwaway pod: kubectl run psql --rm -it --image=postgres:16 -n <ns> -- psql "<dsn>" DeploySource stuck Pending no PostgresWatch with that postgresWatchRef in the same namespace kubectl get postgreswatch -n <ns> No PerformanceRegression appears not enough baseline data, or no deploy event recorded see below Webhook returns 404 wrong path use kubectl get deploysource <name> -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.status.webhookPath}' Webhook returns 401 a webhook secret is set send X-Webhook-Token (Config and Secrets) Webhook times out Service selects no pod, or a NetworkPolicy blocks ingress kubectl get endpoints, kubectl get networkpolicy Manager exits at startup with address already in use the probe port 8081 is taken change --health-probe-bind-address / manager.ports.healthProbe Alerts are not delivered destination policy, egress policy, wrong URL Alerting; check egress to the alert host After helm upgrade, new CRD fields are rejected or ignored Helm does not update CRDs kubectl apply -f deploy/helm/deploylens/crds/ Pod rejected: exceeded quota a ResourceQuota in the namespace kubectl describe resourcequota -n <ns> Pod rejected: violates PodSecurity a namespace policy conflicts with an overridden security context RBAC and access

docs.title: Nothing is detected
docs.text:
"No regression" is often correct, and sometimes means the radar never had what it needs. Work through:

  1. Is the watch running? kubectl get pgw -n <ns> shows Running and a non-zero tracked-queries count. Zero means pg_stat_statements is empty or not enabled.
  2. Is there a deploy event? For sourceType: kubernetes, a rollout must have completed on a new revision: kubectl rollout status deployment/<app> -n <ns>. For webhooks, check the sender's logs and the /events listing.
  3. Is there enough history before the deploy? The radar needs several scrapes of the query running normally before a change means anything. In the lab that is about three minutes; in production it is bounded by windowMinutes and minSamples.
  4. Is the query running enough? minExecutions filters out queries that run too rarely.
  5. Is the change big enough? latencyChangeThreshold is the minimum relative change ("0.20" is 20%).

A PerformanceRegression with status: InsufficientData means the radar considered the deploy and did not have enough samples to decide, which is different from NoRegression. See Detection Algorithm for the thresholds.

docs.title: Collecting a report
docs.text:
When you ask for help, this is what makes the answer fast:

kubectl get pods,deployment,service -n <ns> -o wide
kubectl get postgreswatch,deploysource,performanceregression -n <ns>
kubectl describe postgreswatch <name> -n <ns>
kubectl logs -n <ns> -l app.kubernetes.io/component=manager --tail=200 --prefix
kubectl get events -n <ns> --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
helm get values <release> -n <ns>          # redact the DSN and any secrets first

Redact before you paste

helm get values, kubectl get secret -o yaml and a PostgresWatch with an inline DSN all contain credentials. Remove them before sharing output.

docs.title: Pods and Deployments
docs.text: What runs the radar, how a rollout works, and why a finished rollout counts as a deploy.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Two things in your cluster are Deployments from the radar's point of view: the radar itself, and the application whose releases it is watching. Understanding Pods, ReplicaSets, Deployments and rollouts explains how the radar starts, how to tell it is healthy, how replicas and failover work, and exactly when a deploy event is recorded.

docs.title: Pods
docs.text:
A Pod is the smallest thing Kubernetes runs: one or more containers sharing a network address and storage. You almost never create a Pod yourself. Pods are disposable: when one dies or is replaced, its replacement has a new name and a new IP.

kubectl get pods -n <ns>
kubectl get pods -n <ns> -o wide     # adds node and pod IP
kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns>   # events, probes, restarts

The columns in kubectl get pods are the first diagnostic you have:

Column Meaning READY containers passing their readiness probe / total. 1/1 is healthy; 0/1 is running but not ready. STATUS Running, Pending (not placed or not started), CrashLoopBackOff (keeps exiting), ImagePullBackOff (cannot fetch the image), Completed (finished, for Jobs). RESTARTS how many times a container was restarted. A growing number is a crash loop even if STATUS says Running right now. AGE time since creation. Useful to tell whether a pod is the new one or the old one during a rollout.

docs.title: Deployments and ReplicaSets
docs.text:
A Deployment declares "run N identical pods from this template, and replace them gradually when the template changes". It does this through ReplicaSets: each version of the pod template gets its own ReplicaSet, and a rollout is the Deployment scaling the new ReplicaSet up while scaling the old one down.

Deployment (replicas: 2, template v2)
├── ReplicaSet orders-api-5d8f...   (template v1)  → scaled down to 0
└── ReplicaSet orders-api-7c4b...   (template v2)  → 2 pods

kubectl get deployment,replicaset,pod -n <ns>
kubectl get deployment <name> -n <ns> -o yaml | less

A StatefulSet is the same idea for pods that need a stable identity and storage (databases are the usual case). The radar treats a StatefulSet's rollouts the same way as a Deployment's.

In pg-regression-radar

mode: manager installs one Deployment named <fullname>-manager; mode: operator installs one named <fullname>. Both are ordinary Deployments: kubectl rollout status, kubectl scale and kubectl logs deployment/<name> all work on them. Both run as a non-root user with a read-only root filesystem by default (Hardening), so there is nothing writable to "fix" inside the container.

docs.title: Rollouts
docs.text:
Changing a Deployment's pod template (a new image tag, a changed environment variable, a new annotation on the template) starts a rollout. Kubernetes creates the new ReplicaSet and shifts pods across, honouring the Deployment's strategy so that a minimum number of pods stay available.

kubectl set image deployment/orders-api api=orders-api:v2 -n <ns>   # triggers a rollout
kubectl rollout status deployment/orders-api -n <ns>                # blocks until it finishes
kubectl rollout history deployment/orders-api -n <ns>               # list revisions
kubectl rollout undo deployment/orders-api -n <ns>                  # go back one revision
kubectl rollout undo deployment/orders-api -n <ns> --to-revision=3

Each rollout gets a revision number, kept in the annotation deployment.kubernetes.io/revision on the Deployment. A rollback with rollout undo is also a new rollout: it reuses the old template but gets a new revision number.

docs.title: Why this is the radar's deploy signal
docs.text:
A DeploySource with sourceType: kubernetes watches your Deployment or StatefulSet directly:

apiVersion: radar.pgregressionradar.io/v1alpha1
kind: DeploySource
metadata:
  name: orders-api
  namespace: <ns>
spec:
  postgresWatchRef: orders
  sourceType: kubernetes
  workloadKind: Deployment      # or StatefulSet
  appName: orders-api           # the workload's own name

The radar records a deploy event when the rollout completes on a new revision, the same condition kubectl rollout status waits for, and not when the template merely changes. The event's revision is the Deployment's revision annotation (or the StatefulSet's status.updateRevision). That has practical consequences:

  • A stuck rollout is not a deploy. If new pods never become Ready, no event is recorded. Check with kubectl rollout status.
  • A rollback is a deploy. kubectl rollout undo finishes a rollout onto a (new) revision, so the radar records one. That is useful: if the undo fixes a regression, the data shows it.
  • Changes that do not touch the pod template are not rollouts. Scaling replicas up or down does not create a revision.

Details of every source type, including webhooks from ArgoCD, Flux and Argo Rollouts, are in Deploy Sources & Webhooks.

docs.title: Health: probes
docs.text:
A liveness probe tells Kubernetes when to restart a container; a readiness probe tells it when to send traffic to the pod and, during a rollout, when to consider the new pod "available". The radar's manager exposes both on its health port:

Probe Path Port (default) liveness /healthz 8081 readiness /readyz 8081

A pod with READY 0/1 and a healthy log usually means the readiness probe is failing. kubectl describe pod shows the probe failures under Events. A port clash on 8081 is the common cause of a manager that exits on startup; see Getting Started.

docs.title: Replicas, leader election and logs
docs.text:
A Deployment's replicas field is how many identical pods run. The radar's manager supports more than one replica for high availability, with leader election: all replicas run, but only the one holding a Lease object does the work, and a standby takes over automatically if the leader dies.

kubectl get deployment <fullname>-manager -n <ns>
kubectl get lease -n <ns>
kubectl get lease -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.holderIdentity}'

Two practical points:

  • kubectl logs deployment/<name> shows one pod's log, picked for you. With several replicas, the interesting log is the leader's. Use the lease's holderIdentity to find the pod, or read each pod: kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns>.
  • A standby pod is not broken. It is Running and READY, and quiet. Only the leader scrapes Postgres and writes PerformanceRegression objects.

See Architecture Overview for when to run more than one replica.

docs.title: Resources: requests and limits
docs.text:
Each container can declare requests (what the scheduler reserves) and limits (the ceiling enforced at runtime). A container that exceeds its memory limit is killed (OOMKilled); one that exceeds its CPU limit is throttled, not killed.

resources:
  requests: { cpu: 50m, memory: 64Mi }
  limits:   { cpu: 200m, memory: 128Mi }

50m means 50 millicores, a twentieth of a CPU. The chart exposes these through resources (operator mode) and manager.resources (manager mode), and can also render a ResourceQuota and a LimitRange for the namespace (Hardening). If a pod is rejected with exceeded quota, that quota is the reason.

kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns> | grep -A4 "Last State"      # shows OOMKilled and exit codes
kubectl top pod -n <ns>                                          # needs metrics-server
